source.title: Understanding overfitting peaks in generalization error: Analytical risk curves for l2 and l1 penalized interpolation

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure text are flattened or garbled in the web extraction, but the document is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and simulates risk curves for a synthetic sparse linear-regression model. It refines the interpretation of overfitting peaks by showing that the peak can be separate from the point where generalization becomes good, and that behavior depends on the penalty.
record.gate_note: The paper tests risk as fitting degrees of freedom vary, including analytical and numerical results. It does not test deep networks, training epochs, or increasing sample size as the intervention. It cites findings from other work, which are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Analytical risk curves plus simulations for misparametrized sparse linear regression (MiSpaR) as fitting parameters p vary relative to samples m. They show an overfitting peak at p = m under noise, a second descent that is finite and penalty-dependent, and dissociate the peak from where good generalization starts. These results bear on V4 and V6 in a non-deep model class.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the overfitting peak at interpolation (μ = 1) can be dissociated from the onset of good generalization (μα = 1), which complicates the classical/modern-regime reading. They also conclude that interpolation's generalization depends strongly on the penalty (l1 vs l2), and that infinite overparametrization does not generalize (GE → 1).
record.recipe_differences: Analytical and numerical risk curves for synthetic misparametrized sparse linear regression with l1 and l2 penalties, rather than experiments on deep networks or the original studies' model settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The curve depends on penalty (l1 versus l2), noise variance σ, undersampling α, sparsity ρ, and regularization λ; the location of good generalization can be before or after the μ = 1 peak.

fits_no_version.finding: The overfitting peak at interpolation (μ = 1) is dissociated from the onset of good generalization, which occurs at p = n (μα = 1). Good generalization can start before or after the peak depending on α.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak does not mark the boundary between a classical and a modern regime; where good generalization starts is set by matching the generative model's dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: Behaviour right of the peak depends strongly on the penalty. l1 interpolation generalizes well over a wide range where l2 interpolation is near GE = 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benefits of interpolation past the threshold depend on inductive bias, not on interpolation itself.

record.problems: The main evidence is for a synthetic linear-regression model and asymptotic analytical curves, not deep networks. Numerical simulations are reported with 100 draws, but the text does not give numerical standard-error values. The l1 analysis gives explicit results only in specified regimes.

untested.parts: Sample count is not used as an intervention to show more data hurting near the threshold.
Only one model class (linear regression with l1/l2 penalties); other model classes untested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epoch and sample axes.
Multiple or triple peaks, and elimination of the peak under optimally tuned regularization.
No re-expression of complexity as an effective parameter count.

missing.what: With σ = 0 and α < 1, an effective-noise peak from unobserved parameters appears at μ = 1. With α > 1 there is no noise peak, and GE reaches 0 at μ = 1/α < 1.
GE(μ → ∞) = 1 for both l2 and l1 penalized interpolation with σ > 0. Also, for σ = 0, α < 1, the l2 minimum is 1 − α at μ = 1/α, rising afterwards.
Fig. 1/3 contrast: the overfitting peak is much larger for α < 1 than for α > 1.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source; the study cites Belkin et al. as motivation. V5 was removed from the rows: peak at p = m on one axis does not test a cross-axis complexity measure, and the reader's V5 'challenges' misread the dissociation finding, which now sits under fits_no_version. The reader's V6 limits_scope for r5 was replaced, because optimal tuning being untested belongs under untested, not limits_scope. Results are asymptotic analytics with n = 200 simulations; standard errors are shown graphically only.

versions.untested_parts: Increasing the number of training samples near the interpolation threshold.
The paper studies one synthetic linear-regression model class, not a range of model classes; behavior under other models and settings is untested.
The paper studies fitting degrees of freedom, not epochs or sample-size axes, and does not establish a single effective-complexity measure across axes.
The paper does not test multiple or triple peaks, nor whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates the peak. It reports suppression at finite regularization, not optimal tuning.
It does not re-express complexity using an effective parameter count to test whether the curve becomes an ordinary U-shape.

rows.subject: MiSpaR
rows.size_stated: n, p, and m tend to infinity with ratios fixed for the analytical result; simulations use n = 200
rows.operation_detail: Varied fitting-model size through μ = p/m and derived the l2 penalized interpolation risk curve.
rows.measure: Generalization error (GE) as a function of μ; the paper reports an overfitting peak at μ = 1, with GE ∼ |1 − μ|⁻¹ near μ = 1. It also reports that the start of good generalization is at μα = 1, which can be before or after the peak.
rows.value: Peak at μ = 1; GE ∼ |1 − μ|⁻¹ near μ = 1; good generalization starts at μα = 1 for small σ.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for the analytical result
rows.note: The paper's analytical result concerns a synthetic sparse linear-regression model, not a deep network. The distinction between μ = 1 and μα = 1 is central to its refinement.
rows.check: Removed V5. Peak location at interpolation on a single size axis does not test a single cross-axis complexity measure. The peak-versus-good-generalization dissociation is about interpreting the regimes, not about where the peak sits.

rows.size_stated: n, p, and m tend to infinity with ratios fixed for the analytical result; simulations use n = 200

rows.measure: Generalization error (GE) as a function of μ; the paper reports the overfitting peak at μ = 1, with GE ∼ |1 − μ|⁻¹ near μ = 1. It also reports that the start of good generalization is at μα = 1, which can be before or after the peak.

rows.locator: Sections 1.1 and 3.3.3, especially Eq. 9 and the discussion of the μ > 1 regime

rows.check: Removed V5 for the same reason as r1. For the l1 penalty, the μ ≳ 1 peak shape (Eq. 10) is only approximate.

rows.subject: MiSpaR
rows.size_stated: n, p, and m tend to infinity with ratios fixed
rows.operation_detail: Varied fitting-model size through μ = p/m and evaluated the l2 interpolation risk beyond μ = 1.
rows.measure: Generalization error (GE) as a function of μ.
rows.value: GE2 = 1 − 1/μ for μ > 1 and μα > 1; GE2 > 0 in this regime.
rows.note: For this stated noise-free, α > 1 condition, the l2 risk increases with μ after interpolation rather than improving with further size.
rows.check: Also bears on V6. With σ = 0 and α > 1 there is no noise peak and GE rises past interpolation. This fits a noise-driven peak, and for V4 the risk worsens rather than improving. State 'reversed' applies to V4; for V6 the absence of a peak without noise is as predicted.

source_check.correct: V4: reversed. V6: observed noise dependence; the noise peak is absent when σ = 0 and α > 1.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3.4, Cases 1–2, especially the l2 formula and following paragraph.
source_check.problem: The shared reversed state fits V4, but does not fit the row's additional V6 link.

rows.subject: MiSpaR
rows.size_stated: n, p, and m tend to infinity with ratios fixed
rows.operation_detail: Varied fitting-model size through μ = p/m and derived the l1 interpolation risk curve.
rows.measure: Generalization error (GE) as a function of μ.
rows.value: GE1 = 0 for 1/α < μ < μc(α/ρ); GE1 rises quadratically from zero for μ > μc and GE1(μ → ∞) = 1. For small α/ρ, μc ≈ √(πα/(2ρ)) exp(α/(2ρ)).
rows.note: The l1 result shows improved generalization beyond interpolation over a range of model sizes, but that range ends at μc, after which the risk rises.
rows.check: The row should note that for α < 1 (e.g. α = 0.8, ρ = 0.2) an effective-noise peak appears at μ = 1. GE1 then drops to 0 over 1/α < μ < μc ≈ 18.7 before rising to 1. So the second descent is strong but bounded.

source_check.locator_found: Section 1.1, point 5; Section 3.3.4, zero-error interval, Eq. 20 and final paragraphs.

rows.measure: Generalization-error curve and the overfitting peak.
rows.value: The paper states that the overfitting peak is suppressed at finite values of λ; Figure 1 compares theory and simulation at λ = 0.1 for l2.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors across the 100 trials are shown; numerical values not stated.
rows.locator: Section 1.1, point 3; Figure 1 caption and panels C and F
rows.note: Suppression at finite regularization is reported, but optimal tuning is not tested.
rows.check: Suppression of the peak at finite λ is stated, but the λ = 0.1 figure gives no numbers. The 'partial' state reflects only the untested optimal-tuning part; the direction matches V6.

relationships.condition: MiSpaR, λ → 0, σ > 0 (l2 and l1) and σ = 0 with α < 1, near and just past μ = 1
relationships.reason: GE diverges at μ = 1 (∼|1−μ|⁻¹) and falls again for μ > 1, giving a non-monotonic risk curve in linear regression (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Generalization error diverged as |1−μ|⁻¹ at μ=1 and declined for μ>1.
